say: Why does ninety paise matter? That is roughly what Blinkit kept from every hundred rupees of orders, after discounts, last quarter, on the company's own measure of profit.
Blinkit is Eternal's ten minute delivery app. A year earlier, on that same measure, it lost one hundred and fifty six crore. This time it made one hundred and eighty four crore.
Now the strange part. The longest answer in Eternal's new letter to shareholders, by our count, is about computer programs that shop for you.
Our question: when a computer can do your shopping, what part of Blinkit can it not skip?

First, where does the money come from? Eternal runs four main businesses. Zomato delivers restaurant food. Blinkit delivers goods from small warehouses it calls dark stores. District books tables and tickets. Hyperpure supplies restaurants.

Across the whole group, on that same company measure, called adjusted EBITDA, it came to six hundred and sixty six crore. That is nearly three times a year ago. The measure adds back staff share awards, two hundred and sixty two crore.
So which business made most of it? Not Blinkit. Food delivery: six hundred and twenty seven crore. By our arithmetic, that is ninety four percent of the group total, with losses elsewhere netted off.

Food delivery keeps about five and a half rupees from every hundred of orders, on that measure. Blinkit's orders are much bigger in total, twenty thousand nine hundred and forty crore, but it keeps ninety paise. District still loses money.
Here is a twist. On the unaudited standard accounts, profit for the quarter was one hundred and twenty five crore. Tax was one hundred and ninety eight crore. More than the profit itself.

Why? The letter's note says the parent company's old losses will be fully used up this financial year. The subsidiaries behind Blinkit, Hyperpure and District still carry old losses, to set against their own future profits.
On its own, the parent paid tax of about a quarter of its pre-tax profit, by our arithmetic. Our reading: that is why group tax looks so heavy.

Eternal's revenue jumped seventy six percent on its adjusted measure. Part of that is a change in how Blinkit sells: it now owns more of its inventory, so revenue counts full prices, not a fee. Like for like, the company says, it is fifty eight percent.
So why does ninety paise matter? Because of the direction. The letter says Blinkit's margin has now improved for six quarters in a row.
And the letter gives a glimpse of a grown up Blinkit. Quote: Our mature cities already operate at over five percent adjusted EBITDA margin.
The letter says cities with about seventy percent of its order value are already in profit on that measure.
Why would a bigger network earn more? One idea in the letter is density. Quote: As density builds, our cost to serve each order falls.
Our reading, in plain words: more orders near the same store keep the same shelves and riders busier.
So how fast is it building? Three hundred and eight net new stores in the quarter. Two thousand seven hundred and fifty one in all. It now expects to cross three thousand five hundred by March.
By our arithmetic, that is about seven hundred and fifty more stores in six months.

Will small towns order like big cities? Most new stores will go to smaller cities and newer categories. In smaller cities, the letter says, new stores reach a thousand orders a day about as fast as in metros, with average orders eighty five to ninety percent of metro size.
There is a cost. New stores pull margins down in their first months, the letter says. It expects its more mature stores and cities to more than make up for it.
All of this assumes people keep opening the app. What if a computer does the shopping instead?
Here is the idea the letter is answering: AI agents become the default way to shop, and platforms that do not adapt get cut out. The letter calls that simplistic.
Of its answers, three matter most here. One: is food shopping a chore? It says no. Its surveys say over sixty five percent of Zomato app opens are exploratory.
Those users browse an average of twelve menus and over a hundred food images before ordering. That kind of browsing, the letter says, is hard for an agent.
The letter does admit one chore: repeat orders. Yet reordered carts, it says, are in low single digits on both apps.
Two: an agent can only skip a platform if the product exists without it. A restaurant table exists without District. So does a concert ticket that District does not sell exclusively.
But a meal delivered within minutes, or groceries in ten, does not, the letter says. It takes restaurant kitchens, riders, dark stores and inventory, each step depending on the last.
Three: someone has to fix it when it goes wrong. A missing item. A spilled meal. Quote: An agent can place an order, but it cannot own the outcome.
The verdict. Quote: Blinkit and Zomato sit in the low-risk zone against the threat of agentic commerce. District, it says, sits in the medium to high risk zone.
So where does Eternal say its moat is? Quote: Agents will weaken content moats and strengthen supply chain moats.

But. This is the company's own argument, about its own business. And the letter says so. Quote: We are conscious that as incumbents, we may be predisposed to see resilience where others see vulnerability.

The letter itself says it is watching other markets first. And the filings leave things out. They show total capital spending, nine hundred and forty one crore this quarter, but no cost per new store, no payback figure, no market share figure.

And the letter's very first answer is about its own AI assistant, dark dot AI, which it says is private. It hopes to launch globally within twenty twenty six. It gives no price and no spending figure.

Meanwhile, the group's cash balance fell by one thousand eight hundred and thirteen crore, to sixteen thousand four hundred and seventy five crore. The letter says the main driver was festive inventory and the timing of restaurant payments.

And the letter says agents could make some categories winner takes all, favouring whoever executes best. Food delivery, meanwhile, still supplies about ninety four percent of group profit on this measure, by our arithmetic.
So, back to ninety paise. Our reading of the letter: the bet is that what a computer cannot skip is the physical part. The store nearby. The rider. The shelf that already holds your item.

The company expects that margin to keep improving while it builds. The next checkpoint is March, when it says it will cross three thousand five hundred stores. Its next letters will show whether the ninety paise keeps growing.
